system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 9 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2154-08-06 18:40:00 to 2154-08-14 19:02:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of type 2 diabetes, end-stage renal disease with two kidney transplants, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, peripheral arterial disease with left below-knee amputation, and obstructive sleep apnea was admitted for hypertensive urgency with systolic blood pressures reaching 244 mmHg, associated with chest tightness and mild pulmonary edema. The episode was partly attributed to unintentional underdosing of labetalol due to a change in tablet strength. He also experienced transient epigastric pain concerning for mesenteric ischemia, though workup was negative. His blood pressure was stabilized with IV nitroglycerin initially, followed by transition to oral amlodipine, doxazosin, hydralazine, and increased labetalol, while nifedipine was discontinued. He received IV furosemide for pulmonary congestion and was transitioned back to home torsemide. His platelet count, which dipped during admission, normalized. He was discharged home on an adjusted antihypertensive regimen with close follow-up for transplant care, sleep apnea reassessment, and monitoring of kidney mass and medication levels.
problems: Acute on chronic diastolic (congestive) heart failure
Type 2 diabetes mellitus with diabetic nephropathy
Pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease
Peripheral artery disease with left below knee amputation

procedures.long_title: Insertion of Monitoring Device into Pulmonary Trunk, Percutaneous Approach

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Johnson. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You were brought in today because you’ve been feeling short of breath and fatigued. Is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I’ve been really tired and can’t catch my breath, even when I’m just sitting. My legs also feel heavy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Given your history with heart failure and kidney transplants, we’re concerned that your heart isn’t handling fluid well. We’ve checked your labs and a chest X-ray shows some fluid in your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s not good. Is that why I feel so puffed out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your heart pumps fine, but it’s stiff and doesn’t relax well, so fluid backs up. We’re starting you on a diuretic through the IV to help remove the extra fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. My blood pressure’s been all over the place too. Sometimes I feel dizzy and stop my meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noticed your BP has been labile—spiking into the 200s and dropping low. We’ll adjust your medications carefully. But stopping them when you feel dizzy can make things worse. We’ll set a safe lower limit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s the safe number? I don’t want to pass out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll say: if your systolic is below 100 or your diastolic below 60, you can hold your hydralazine. But keep taking the others unless we say otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your ultrasound of the transplanted kidney shows it’s functioning well, though the blood flow resistance is a bit high. It’s improved from last time, so that’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that because of the fluid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. Fluid overload stresses the kidney. We’re working with nephrology to balance diuresis without hurting your transplant function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my creatinine was high—5.6. Is that bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s elevated, but it’s come down to 5.3, which is a positive sign. We’ll keep monitoring it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound of your liver and abdomen. Your liver is fatty but no serious issues. We saw a small cyst and a bit of fluid in the belly, which fits with your heart condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had belly pain too. Could that be from the fluid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We checked for infections and pancreatitis—your blood cultures were negative, and your pancreatic enzymes are fine. It’s likely related to the heart failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the body aches? I thought it was from the Bumex I used before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We switched you to Lasix IV, and your aches have improved. It may have been a reaction to Bumex. We’ll keep you on Lasix for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your echocardiogram shows your heart is pumping well—ejection fraction is 70%—but there’s moderate mitral regurgitation and higher pressures in the lungs. This confirms your heart failure diagnosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that worse than before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The mitral leak is a bit worse, and your pulmonary pressure is up. That’s why you’re having more symptoms. We’re adjusting your meds to reduce the strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What meds are changing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adding isosorbide mononitrate once daily to help with blood vessel dilation and reduce heart workload. We’re also starting clonidine twice daily to help stabilize your blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve never taken clonidine. Any side effects?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can cause dry mouth or drowsiness. We’ll start low and watch how you do. If you feel too dizzy, let us know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning a right heart catheterization tomorrow. It’s a test to measure pressures inside your heart and help guide your treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe? I’ve had heart procedures before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s low risk. We’ll use the femoral vein in your groin. You’ll be awake but sedated. The results will help us fine-tune your diuretics and blood pressure meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The cath showed elevated filling pressures, which confirms your heart is struggling to relax. But your overall function is preserved. We’ll transition you from IV Lasix to oral torsemide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can stop the IV?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’re responding well. We’ll send you home on torsemide 60 mg daily. Keep weighing yourself every morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I gain weight, I should call?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—any gain over 3 pounds in a day or two could mean fluid is building up. Call your cardiologist or nephrologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We inserted a small monitoring device into your pulmonary artery yesterday to track pressures. It’s temporary and helps us manage your heart failure more precisely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel it. Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a standard procedure. It was removed after we got the data. No complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked the groin site from your heart cath. The ultrasound shows no pseudoaneurysm or bleeding. All looks clean.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t felt any pain there, so that’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re healing well. Your breathing has improved, and your weight is down. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day. Your discharge weight is 80 kg. You’re breathing much better, and your labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds am I going home on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before, with a few changes: we’ve added clonidine twice daily and isosorbide mononitrate once daily. Keep taking your torsemide, labetalol, amlodipine, and the rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I hold hydralazine if my BP is under 100/60?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Write that down. Also, check your blood sugar regularly and take your insulin as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. What about my sleep apnea? I still can’t use the CPAP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve referred you for a new sleep study. You may need BIPAP instead. Keep using your oxygen at night—3 liters.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You also need a repeat kidney ultrasound in a year to monitor a small cyst. And get your labs done—chemistry panel and tacrolimus level—one hour before your morning dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Who do I see for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Dr. Patel in nephrology. Your appointment is scheduled. If you feel short of breath, dizzy, or gain weight quickly, call them or come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Breathing easier. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Remember: weigh yourself daily, take your meds, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve got it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, one last thing—my sister is picking me up. Can she get the discharge papers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she can sign for them at the desk. Make sure she has ID.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And call the HeartLine if you have urgent questions—especially about breathing or chest discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep that number handy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, you’re all set. Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick follow-up call—just checking in. How’s your breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still good. I weighed myself—same as this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Another check-in. Any dizziness or side effects from the new meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No dizziness. Clonidine’s making me a bit dry-mouthed, but it’s okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. Sip water or use sugar-free gum. Call if it bothers you too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final call for today. You’re doing well. We’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again. Feeling much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming you made it home safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. All good. Thanks for checking.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of type 2 diabetes, end-stage renal disease with two kidney transplants, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, and obstructive sleep apnea was admitted for fatigue and shortness of breath due to acute on chronic heart failure with fluid overload. He was started on IV diuresis with Lasix, which was later transitioned to oral torsemide. His blood pressure was labile, prompting adjustments to his antihypertensive regimen, including the addition of clonidine and isosorbide mononitrate. A right heart catheterization confirmed elevated filling pressures, and a pulmonary artery monitoring device was temporarily inserted to guide management. His symptoms improved, and he was discharged home on optimized medical therapy with instructions to monitor weight, hold hydralazine if blood pressure dropped below 100/60, and follow up with nephrology and cardiology. Outpatient sleep study and repeat renal ultrasound were recommended.
